items.text: Our town should build a skate park.
Homework on weekends does more harm than good.
Every student needs to learn first aid.
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
Our school day starts at 8:15.
Canada has ten provinces.
Pizza is the tastiest food.
I love rainy days.
Purple is the prettiest colour.

title: Make it a claim
instructions: Choose the word that turns each sentence into a claim someone could argue about.

items.sentence: Schools ___ start later in the morning.
items.hint: Which word says what ought to happen?
items.explanation: “Should” makes it a position you have to prove.

items.hint: Which word asks for a change?
items.explanation: Calling for a ban takes a side.

items.sentence: Learning outdoors is ___ than learning in a classroom for science.
items.hint: Which word judges one thing against another?
items.explanation: “Better” is a judgement someone could argue with.

items.sentence: Every school ___ teach students how to cook.
items.hint: Which word makes a strong demand?

questions.prompt: Why can’t a fact be a thesis?

options.text: There is nothing to prove: anyone can check it

questions.explanation: A thesis needs to be something you prove or explain.

questions.prompt: Which is a claim?

options.text: Students should have a say in the school menu.

questions.explanation: A takes a side someone could disagree with.

questions.prompt: How do you turn “I hate long car rides” into a claim?

options.text: Families should take breaks every hour on long car rides.
I really, really hate long car rides.

questions.explanation: A says what should happen, and could be proved with reasons.

title: Opinions into claims
prompt: Turn each opinion into a claim someone could disagree with. Write one claim for each task listed above the writing box.
tips: Use should, must, need to, better or ban.
Add “because …” to show you could prove it.

sentences.ask: Opinion: “I love dogs.” Write a claim about dogs (… should … because …).
Opinion: “Summer is the best season.” Write a claim about summer holidays.
Opinion: “Video games are awesome.” Write a claim about video games.

title: Strong thesis?
instructions: Sort each sentence: is it a strong argumentative thesis, too vague, or not a thesis at all?

items.text: Schools should ban junk food because it harms health, focus and behaviour.
Our library should open on Sundays because families are free, students need study space and books get used more.
Every student should learn to swim because it saves lives, builds fitness and opens up new sports.
Junk food is a big issue.
Libraries are good for many reasons.
Swimming is something people have opinions about.
In this essay I will talk about junk food.
Our library has 12,000 books.

title: Complete the thesis
instructions: Choose the reason that best completes each thesis.

items.sentence: Schools should have gardens because they teach science, ___ and bring students together.
items.hint: Which reason could be its own body paragraph?
items.explanation: It is specific and provable, like the other two reasons.

items.sentence: Students should walk to school because it builds fitness, ___ and gives them time to wake up.
items.hint: Which one is a real benefit you could prove?
items.explanation: Fewer cars at the gate is a benefit you can show with evidence.

items.sentence: Every school should teach music because it ___, builds teamwork and gives students a creative outlet.
items.hint: Which reason is a benefit for students?
items.explanation: Studies link music lessons to memory; that’s provable.

questions.prompt: Which thesis maps out three body paragraphs?

options.text: Cities should plant more trees because trees cool streets, clean the air and calm people.
Trees are nice to have in cities.

questions.explanation: Three reasons, three body paragraphs: cool, clean, calm.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with “Phones are a big issue in schools.”?

options.text: It doesn’t take a side or say what should happen

questions.explanation: A thesis takes a clear position.

questions.prompt: How many sentences should a thesis usually be?
questions.explanation: One clear sentence that the whole essay proves.

title: Three argumentative theses
prompt: Write one argumentative thesis for each question listed above the writing box. Each takes a side and gives reasons with “because”.
tips: Choose the side you could prove best.
Make each reason specific enough for its own body paragraph.

sentences.ask: Should kids get a weekly allowance?

title: Argue, explain or tell?
instructions: Sort each thesis by the kind of essay it belongs to.

items.text: Our school should start a recycling club because it would cut waste and teach good habits.
Video games deserve a place in classrooms because they teach problem-solving.
Recycling works in four steps: collecting, sorting, cleaning and remaking.
Earthquakes have three main causes.
Social media affects teenagers in several ways.
The day I forgot my lines in the school play taught me to laugh at myself.
When my brother was born, I learned what it means to be patient.
Losing my first football match changed how I think about winning.

title: From topic to thesis
instructions: Each sentence just names a topic. Rewrite it as an informative thesis that names the parts.

items.explanation: Volcanoes form in three stages. Now the reader knows what the body paragraphs will cover.

items.task: Use the parts given: “in three ways”.
items.source: My topic is how bees help farms.
answers: Bees help farms in three ways.
items.explanation: Bees help farms in three ways.

items.task: Use the parts given: “in several ways”.
items.source: I am going to explain sleep and learning.
answers: Sleep affects learning in several ways.
items.explanation: Sleep affects learning in several ways.

questions.prompt: Which is an informative thesis?

options.text: Bicycles work through three simple machines: wheels, levers and gears.
Everyone should ride a bike to school.
I got my first bike when I was six.

questions.explanation: It explains a topic and names the parts. B argues; C is just an event.

questions.prompt: What makes a narrative focus different from just telling an event?

options.text: It says what the event meant or taught you

questions.explanation: “I moved house” is an event. “Moving house taught me to make friends fast” is a focus.

questions.prompt: Should an informative thesis take a side?

options.text: No: it explains, it doesn’t argue
Only if the topic is sport

questions.explanation: Informative essays teach the reader; argumentative essays take sides.

title: Explain and tell
prompt: Write three theses, one for each task listed above the writing box: two informative theses and one narrative focus.
tips: Informative: … in three ways. / … has three main causes. / … works in four steps.
Narrative: The day I … taught me … / When I …, I learned …

sentences.ask: Informative: how exercise helps the body (name the parts or say how many ways).
Informative: how a topic you know well works (a game, a recipe, a machine).
Narrative focus: a true moment from your life and what it taught you.

title: Name the hook
instructions: Sort each hook by its kind.

items.text: Have you ever wondered where your rubbish goes?
Imagine a school with no bells.
Every minute, a truckload of plastic enters the ocean.
Nearly half of all food grown is never eaten.
“Education is the most powerful weapon you can use to change the world,” said Nelson Mandela.
“Play is the work of childhood,” wrote the teacher Maria Montessori.
When I was seven, I lost my dog at the beach.
One morning last spring, our classroom flooded.

title: Finish the hook
instructions: Choose the words that make each hook grab the reader.

items.sentence: ___ tried to study with a phone buzzing beside you?
items.hint: Start a question that pulls the reader in.
items.explanation: “Have you ever…?” makes the reader picture it.

items.sentence: Every year, ___ of school lunches end up in the bin.
items.hint: Which one is surprising and specific?

items.sentence: ___, I stood at the edge of the pool, too scared to jump.
items.explanation: A short-story hook drops the reader into a moment.

items.sentence: ___ a city where every roof is a garden.
items.hint: Ask the reader to see something.
items.explanation: “Imagine…” invites the reader into the idea.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a hook?

options.text: Hello! My essay is about bees.
Without bees, there would be no apples.
What would breakfast look like without bees?

questions.explanation: An announcement tells the reader what you’ll do. B and C make them curious.

questions.prompt: Which hook is a bold statement?

options.text: Have you ever had too much homework?
When I was ten, I cried over homework.

questions.explanation: Short and strong. B is a question; C is a short story.

questions.prompt: An essay argues for longer lunch breaks. Which hook fits best?

options.text: Have you ever had to swallow your sandwich in five minutes flat?

questions.explanation: A leads straight to the topic. B is off topic; C is an announcement.

title: Three hooks, one topic
prompt: Topic: should schools have a four-day week? Write three different hooks for an essay on this topic, one for each task listed above the writing box.
tips: Question: Have you ever…? / What if…? / Imagine…
Surprising fact: use a number (you may invent a realistic one for practice).
Short story: When I…, / One Friday…, / Last year…

sentences.ask: A surprising-fact hook with a number.
A short-story hook: a tiny true (or realistic) moment.

title: Build the funnel
instructions: Put these sentences in order to make an introduction: hook, background, thesis.

items.text: Have you ever seen a turtle tangled in a plastic bag?
Turtles often mistake floating bags for jellyfish, their favourite food.
Every year, millions of bags blow from streets into rivers and the sea.
Our city should ban plastic bags because they harm wildlife, clog drains and are easy to replace.

explanation: The question hooks; the two background sentences explain the problem; the thesis comes last and takes a side.

title: Good background?
instructions: An introduction argues: “Our school should have a longer lunch break because students need time to eat, rest and play.” Sort each sentence.

buckets.label: Save it for a body paragraph

items.text: At our school, lunch lasts just twenty minutes.
By the time students get through the lunch line, half of that time is gone.
For example, my friend Leo never finishes his sandwich.
A study found that students who play at lunch focus better in the afternoon.
My favourite food is spaghetti.
The school gym was painted blue last year.

questions.prompt: Where does background go?

options.text: Between the hook and the thesis

questions.explanation: Background is the bridge from hook to thesis.

questions.prompt: What does background give the reader?

options.text: What they need to know to understand the thesis

questions.explanation: The situation, the problem or a key fact; save the evidence for the body.

questions.prompt: How long should background usually be?
questions.explanation: Enough to set the scene, then get to the thesis.

title: Hook, bridge, thesis
prompt: Topic: should students be allowed to bring pets to school one day a year? Write a four-sentence introduction, one sentence for each task listed above the writing box.
tips: Hook: a question, a surprising fact, a quote, a short story or a bold statement.
Background: what is the situation now? What does the reader need to know?

sentences.ask: A hook that grabs the reader.
Background: the situation now (for example, what the school rules say).
More background: why this matters to students or families.
Your thesis: your side and your reasons.

title: Label the introduction
instructions: These sentences come from two introductions, one about reading and one about volcanoes. Sort each into its part.

items.text: What if twenty minutes a day could make you a better student in every subject?
Many students stop reading for fun when they start middle school.
Every school should set aside time for free reading because it builds vocabulary, focus and imagination.
In 1980, Mount St. Helens blew off the top 400 metres of its peak.
Volcanoes form where hot, melted rock from deep underground pushes up through the Earth’s crust.
There are about 1,350 active volcanoes in the world today.
Volcanoes form in three stages: melting, rising and erupting.

title: Order a narrative introduction
instructions: Put these sentences in order to make the introduction to a narrative essay.

items.text: I still remember the smell of chlorine on the morning of my first swim race.
I was nine, and I had only learned to swim that summer.
My whole family had come to watch, and my legs would not stop shaking.
That race taught me that being scared is not the same as being stuck.

explanation: A short-story hook, background that sets the scene, then the focus: what the story meant.

questions.prompt: What is the right order for an introduction?
questions.explanation: Wide to narrow, like a funnel: the thesis comes last.

questions.prompt: Why put the thesis at the end of the introduction?

options.text: It leads straight into the body paragraphs that prove it
Because it is the least important sentence

questions.explanation: The last thing the reader reads before the body is your main point.

questions.prompt: An introduction has a great hook and a thesis but nothing between them. What should you add?

options.text: A sentence or two of background

questions.explanation: Background bridges the hook and the thesis.

title: Write an introduction
prompt: Should students be allowed to use phones at lunch? Write the introduction to an argumentative essay on this question: a hook, one to three sentences of background, and your thesis last. One paragraph. Then check your essay map.
tips: Pick a hook that fits: a question, a surprising fact, a quote, a short story or a bold statement.
Background: what are the rules now? Why are people talking about it?

title: Thesis & Introduction check
instructions: Ten questions on everything in this unit. You need 8 or more right (80%) to pass. If you don’t pass, you’ll see what to review and get new questions to try again.

questions.prompt: Which is a claim?

options.text: Our town should plant a tree for every new house.

questions.explanation: A takes a side. B is a fact; C is an opinion.

questions.prompt: Which is a fact?

options.text: The Pacific is the largest ocean.

questions.explanation: It can be checked.

questions.prompt: Which is an opinion (personal taste)?
questions.explanation: Nobody can prove what tastes best.

questions.prompt: Which word often signals a claim?
questions.explanation: Should, must, need to, better and ban all take a position.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest argumentative thesis?

options.text: Students should learn first aid because it saves lives, builds confidence and helps families.
First aid is a big topic.
I am going to write about first aid.

questions.explanation: A claim plus three reasons.

questions.prompt: In an argumentative thesis, what usually comes after “because”?
questions.explanation: Claim + because + reasons.

questions.prompt: A thesis lists three reasons. What will the body paragraphs be about?

options.text: One reason each, in the same order

questions.explanation: The thesis maps out the essay.

questions.prompt: What makes “Sports are good.” a weak thesis?

options.text: It is too vague: good how, for whom, so what?

questions.explanation: A strong thesis is specific and says what should happen.

questions.prompt: Which is an informative thesis?
questions.explanation: It names the topic and its parts without taking a side.

questions.prompt: Which is a narrative focus?

options.text: The day I got lost in the city taught me to stay calm.

questions.explanation: A true moment plus what it meant.

questions.prompt: Turn “This essay is about earthquakes” into an informative thesis.
questions.explanation: Topic + parts.

questions.prompt: What does a narrative focus tell the reader?

options.text: What the story taught or changed

questions.explanation: The story shows it; the focus names it.

questions.prompt: Which is a question hook?

options.text: What would you do with one extra hour every day?
In this essay I will discuss time.

questions.explanation: It makes the reader think.

questions.prompt: Which is a surprising-fact hook?

options.text: The average person spends six months of their life waiting at red lights.
Traffic lights are red, amber and green.
Have you been in a car?

questions.explanation: A number that makes you sit up.

questions.prompt: Why is “Hello, my essay is about pets” a poor opening?

options.text: It announces instead of grabbing the reader

questions.explanation: Start with something that makes the reader curious.

questions.prompt: Which hook best fits a narrative essay about a camping trip?

options.text: At midnight, something scratched at our tent.

questions.explanation: A short-story hook drops the reader into the moment.

questions.prompt: What must a quote hook include?

options.text: Quotation marks and who said it

questions.explanation: Show the exact words and give credit.

questions.prompt: Where does background go?

options.text: Between the hook and the thesis

questions.explanation: It bridges the two.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is good background for “Our school should start a recycling club”?

options.text: Right now, our school has only two recycling bins for 600 students.

questions.explanation: It explains the situation that makes the thesis needed.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in a body paragraph, not the background?

options.text: For example, the club at Hill School collected 2,000 cans in a month.
Many schools throw away tons of paper.
Recycling has become a hot topic.

questions.explanation: Specific evidence proves a reason, so save it for the body.

questions.prompt: What is the right order for an introduction?
questions.explanation: A funnel: wide to narrow.

questions.prompt: Where should the thesis be?

options.text: The last sentence of the introduction
The first sentence of the introduction

questions.explanation: It leads into the body.

questions.prompt: Your essay map shows “! No background yet”. What should you do?

options.text: Add a sentence or two of context between the hook and the thesis

questions.explanation: Background is the bridge.

questions.prompt: How long is a typical introduction?

options.text: One paragraph of about three to five sentences

questions.explanation: Hook, background, thesis: one paragraph.

title: Write an informative introduction
prompt: Write the introduction to an informative essay explaining how sleep affects students’ learning: a hook (a surprising fact works well), one to three sentences of background, and a thesis last that names the parts you would explain. One paragraph. Then check your essay map.
tips: Informative: explain, don’t argue. Your thesis can say “… in three ways” or name the three parts.
Ideas for parts: memory, focus, mood, energy, health.
Background: how much sleep do students need? How much do many get?
